newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong civil service policy dealt a blow.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong civil service policy dealt a blow.

text.p: Hong Kong's effort to localise its civil service have been dealt a blow after a court ruled parts of its policy illegal, a representative of a local civil servants organization said on Saturday.
"The judgement has got a very serous impact on the localisation policy," Hui Kwok-hung, chairman of the Senior Non-Expatriate Officers' Association, told government radio.
Hui said he was seeking talks with the government.

The British colony's administration is working to localise the civil service, a task made more urgent by Hong Kong's return to China in 1997, by nurturing local Chinese officers and more recently by letting expatriate officers transfer to local terms.
Expatriates -- usually from Britain, Australia and New Zealand -- have long sat at the top of the colonial bureaucracy.
But many overseas officers have said they were wrongfully demoted or forced out despite being qualified and permanent residents of Hong Kong, and accused the policy of being unfair.

Hong Kong's Court of Appeal on Friday ruled that parts of the localisation policy breached the territory's Bill of Rights -- including the demotion of overseas officers transferring to local terms, restrictions on promotion and consideration of Chinese-language ability when determining rank.

The ruling overturned a High Court decision last year saying the demotion policy was justified by the government's need to maintain good labour relations with local staff, despite running contrary to the Bill of Rights.
Overseas officers who brought the appeal are now expected pursue compensation claims.
The independent Ming Pao Daily said on Saturday the ruling would dampen the morale of local civil servants.

But the English-language South China Morning Post said the judgement recognised that localisation was right and proper, only requiring the government to restructure the policy so that it did not infringe the law.
There was no immediate reaction from the government.
